transcript_text:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-10-19
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samantha Ortiz (Emerald Works, Head of IT), Derek Wu (Emerald Works, Security Architect), Maya Patel (Emerald Works, Eng Manager)

Summary:
- Intro and scope: Emerald Works evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for user-facing inference with strong compliance constraints (SOC2 + ISO in roadmap).
- Key concerns: SSO/SAML integration, RBAC + least privilege, KMS for envelope encryption, audit logs and retention, and contractual requirements for data residency and retention.
- Next steps: Redwood to provide SOC2/ISO artifacts and schedule a deep technical session for private/dedicated performance and KMS integration.

Topics Tagged: Security posture, SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS/encryption, audit logs, retention policies, dedicated capacity sizing, fallback policies

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, uh, quick intro - I'm Jordan Lee, AE on the Redwood side and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:11] Samantha: Good thanks. We, um, pulled the team together because we need to understand where Redwood fits versus, you know, the cloud vendors and our self-host strategy.
[00:20] Jordan: Great. High level agenda, we'll cover compliance posture, auth and access, encryption/KMS, audit logs + retention, then deployment options and any questions. Sound good?
[00:31] Derek: Sounds good. We'll probably jump to the KMS bit — that's the blocker for us.
[00:35] Priya: Cool. Quick question on scope, are you planning to push PII to hosted endpoints or keep everything inside VPC/private yet?
[00:44] Maya: For the pilot we may route hashed user ids and some pseudonymized content to hosted, but our long term plan is to move to private for PHI and anything regulated.
[00:55] Samantha: Right, we're regulated in EU and US, so data residency and auditability are must-haves.
[01:02] Jordan: Got it. We're SOC 2 Type II compliant and have ISO 27001 assessment artifacts — I'll share the summary and the relevant pages.
[01:11] Derek: Can you confirm SOC2 scope covers both Hosted API and Redwood Dedicated?
[01:16] Jordan: Good question. Our hosted environment is in scope for SOC2; Dedicated pools are included under our control plane compliance, but customers get additional isolation and contractual language. For private installs (VPC/on-prem) we provide the control plane only or a customer-managed control plane depending on the model.
[01:33] Maya: Okay, can you be more specific about logs — like do you provide immutable audit logs and for how long? We need 12 months of tamper-evident logs for infra and access events.
[01:44] Priya: We emit audit trails for admin actions, model rollouts, and token-level access. Logs can be shipped to the customer's SIEM or centralized GCS/S3. Retention is configurable; typical hosted retention is 90 days by default but enterprise plans can extend to 12 months or longer via add-on.
[02:02] Samantha: Is the retention enforced server-side or is it exported and then customer-managed? We need contractual guarantees for retention and deletion on contract end.
[02:13] Jordan: For hosted, we can include retention SLAs via contract and we support deletion requests; for private deployments you control retention since logs can stay in your VPC. We'll put standard deletion language in the SOC2 + contract addendum.
[02:28] Derek: KMS — how does Redwood integrate with customer keys? Do you use envelope encryption? Does Redwood have access to plaintext keys?
[02:36] Priya: We support external KMS via standard integrations — AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, and HSM options for private. We use envelope encryption; the platform does not persist customer root keys. Operational keys (like per-host keys) are rotated and logs capture key usage.
[02:52] Derek: So the private key material never leaves customer KMS?
[02:56] Priya: Correct. For Dedicated and Private, the data keys are wrapped with your CMK; Redwood holds only wrapped keys. For Hosted we can also integrate with a customer-managed KMS using our KMS proxy; there are some performance tradeoffs.
[03:10] Samantha: You said performance tradeoffs — can you quantify? Latency is a hard requirement, sub-200ms p95 for chat endpoints.
[03:19] Priya: The KMS calls add crypto overhead, typically adding 10-40ms depending on region and KMS latency. That's why we recommend caching unwrapped DEKs in memory with TTL and using envelope encryption per-request to avoid synchronous KMS calls for every token. We can show benchmarks in the deep-dive.
[03:38] Maya: That caching — from a security perspective how long do you keep the key in memory? What are the controls?
[03:44] Priya: Short TTLs, locked memory areas, and strict RBAC on the services that can access the DEKs. For higher-assurance customers we run KMS in a way that limits memory residency and rotate more frequently. It's a tradeoff between performance and blast radius.
[03:58] Derek: RBAC — we need granular roles for model deployments, so only a small SRE group can change model rollouts, devs can only create prompts in a staging project. How fine-grained is your access model?
[04:10] Jordan: RBAC supports org/teams/projects, with role definitions that map to admin/engineer/viewer etc. We also support custom roles in enterprise plans and SCIM/SSO provisioning so you can sync groups from your IdP.
[04:22] Samantha: Does Redwood support SAML 2.0 and OIDC? We use Okta.
[04:27] Priya: Yes both. We've seen some customers call it "sammel" so no worries. For Okta we do SAML SSO for the Console and OIDC for service tokens, plus SCIM for group provisioning.
[04:37] Maya: Are session lengths configurable? We need to set shorter sessions for admin roles and enforce MFA.
[04:42] Priya: Yes, session TTLs, IP restrictions, and MFA enforcement can be configured at the org level. We also support RBAC policies that require step-up auth for certain actions.
[04:52] Derek: Auditability — do you provide event hashes or something tamper-evident? We want to feed logs into our WORM storage.
[04:59] Jordan: We can sign audit events and provide event digests. Logs can be exported to your WORM buckets; for hosted we keep originals for the retention window, then purge per policy.
[05:10] Samantha: Data residency — we must ensure EU data stays in EU. What's the model for region pinning?
[05:17] Priya: You can pin requests to region-specific endpoints and models. For hosted we have EU regions and contractual data residency clauses. Dedicated and Private give you full control.
[05:26] Maya: Let's talk about model artifacts — where are model weights stored for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[05:31] Priya: For hosted the model binaries are stored on Redwood-managed infrastructure; for Dedicated we provide isolated pools where the weights are accessible only to that pool and encrypted at rest. For Private/on-prem the customer controls storage.
[05:44] Derek: Any concerns around telemetry or anonymized usage data — do you collect that?
[05:48] Jordan: We collect minimal operational telemetry for SLOs and to improve routing; it's anonymized by default but can be disabled or contractually excluded for enterprise.
[05:57] Samantha: Can we restrict model fallback? We don't want requests routed to cheaper models automatically for regulated data.
[06:03] Priya: Absolutely. Routing policies are configurable per-route and per-tenant. You can disable fallback or restrict to vetted model variants only.
[06:12] Derek: Encryption in transit — TLS is standard, but do you support mutual TLS for service-to-service?
[06:17] Priya: Yes mTLS is supported for private and dedicated inter-service communication; for hosted customer-to-service we use TLS with strong ciphers and client certs for some enterprise customers.
[06:27] Maya: What about pen tests and third-party audits? Are the reports sharable?
[06:31] Jordan: We have third-party penetration tests periodically; summary reports are shareable under an NDA. SOC2 and ISO artifacts come with the compliance package.
[06:40] Derek: Onboarding timeline — if we choose Dedicated, how long to spin up a pool for a pilot?
[06:46] Priya: Typical lead time for Dedicated pilot is 2-4 weeks depending on capacity and networking hoops. Private on-prem will be longer, normally 6-12 weeks depending on hardware procurement and network config.
[06:59] Samantha: Cost is a factor — we may start hosted for a non-PII subset and then move to Dedicated. What are common contractual guardrails for moving data?
[07:08] Jordan: We can include migration playbooks and a data erasure checklist during transition. Also can put explicit clauses to prevent automatic copying of data between environments.
[07:17] Maya: One more — do you support per-tenant encryption keys for multi-tenant pools?
[07:23] Priya: Yes per-tenant wrapping keys are supported; they help reduce blast radius in shared pools.
[07:29] Derek: Ok good. For the deep-dive we want to run a short benchmark with our sample payloads — is that doable?
[07:36] Priya: Yes, please send sample payloads and expected QPS and we'll run against Dedicated and a private-lite config. We'll capture token-level latency and cold-start characteristics.
[07:46] Samantha: We'll also need a compliance checklist for procurement to fast-track approvals.
[07:50] Jordan: We'll send a procurement pack and the SOC2 + ISO excerpts.
[07:54] Maya: Who's the point on your side for privacy/legal questions?
[07:58] Jordan: I'll loop in our legal and compliance contacts after this call; for now I'm the owner.
[08:03] Derek: A few clarifying Qs — do you support customer-managed logging endpoints (syslog/S3) and do you retain the raw access tokens?
[08:12] Priya: Yes customer-managed logging endpoints are supported. We don't retain raw user secrets after processing; tokens are short-lived and rotated. However, some debugging traces may contain masked tokens; we can exclude those by configuration.
[08:28] Samantha: Anything we should expect as surprises in the contract around encryption or incident response?
[08:34] Jordan: Incident response commitments and notification windows are standard in enterprise SLAs. We can add specific clauses for key compromise and data breach handling.
[08:42] Derek: Great. A note on the KMS proxy — will you give us the architecture diagram? We want to validate network flows with our security team.
[08:49] Priya: Yes I'll attach the KMS proxy diagram and a short note about envelope encryption and key rotation.
[08:56] Maya: Timing-wise we want the deeper session next week if possible.
[09:00] Jordan: Priya, do you have availability Thurs or Fri for the deep-dive?
[09:03] Priya: I can do Friday morning PST.
[09:06] Samantha: Friday morning works for us.
[09:08] Jordan: Great. I'll send calendar invite and share initial docs.
[09:12] Derek: One small thing — we use an internal compliance tag for datasets, we want to ensure Redwood preserves that metadata for lineage.
[09:19] Priya: We can preserve metadata in request envelopes and the audit logs; we'll document the fields supported.
[09:25] Samantha: Awesome. Anything else?
[09:28] Jordan: Quick recap — Jordan to send SOC2/ISO excerpts + procurement pack; Priya to schedule deep dive and share benchmark template + KMS proxy diagram; Derek and Maya to share retention policy, PII inventory, and sample payloads.
[09:43] Maya: Thanks all, this was helpful.
[09:46] Jordan: Thanks — we’ll follow up with the artifacts.
